The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

The night page for the fourteenth had five entries, and Maren Ashquill had written four of them.

She knew her own hand the way she knew her own walk, and she knew the office ink. The night the Merrow Bell was lost had entered the parish memory before that autumn gave the loss its second meaning, and the account of it belongs here, as the village would tell it.

She had been a familiar of the port for years: a coasting ketch of ninety tons, broad in the bow, slow and sure, working general cargoes up and down the Hethering coast in all weathers. Her master had used Glasswater Stave through every season and knew the Saltgrass shoals, the village would have said, as well as any man who did not actually fish them. On her last passage she had loaded at Saltern Cross and stood east in the afternoon of as dirty an October day as the year produced, with the glass falling and the wind backing southeast, against the advice — this was remembered later, and weighed — of older masters drinking by the chandlery stove.

The seas had opened her garboards on the first touch of the shoal, he said; she had filled too fast for anything but the boat; she had gone down inside the half hour, in eight fathoms by his own last cast of the lead.

The underwriters' men were in the village within the week, dry men in city coats asking wet questions. CHAPTER XV

They took Severin Quenholt at The Cold Lantern that evening, where he sat at his usual table with his usual glass, agreeing pleasantly with his neighbors about the sad state of the times.

He denied nothing for long; that was the strangest part, the village said afterwards, and the part that made it believable. Confronted in the inn's back parlor with the chronometer, the tobacco-tin accounts, the boat-hook stamped M.B., and the doctor's saucer of violet-blooming ink, he sat quiet for a while with his hands folded, like a merchant checking a column twice, and then he balanced the books aloud.

He had gone to the harbor office late on the fourteenth to reason with Pellow, he said — only to reason, to offer the survey a percentage of its own. The harbormaster had listened with his patient square face and then said he would have the registrar's ledger in on Monday, the original, and the survey held in the open, and the books set side by side; paper was honest, said the harbormaster, even on this quay. Then he had turned to take the chronometer's travelling box down — the survey would need official time, he said, everything would be done by the book — and something in the calm of it, said Quenholt, in the man's untroubled certainty that figures must come right, had risen over him like water over a gauge. The boat-hook had been standing against his own barrow of salvage gear by the door. He did not remember deciding.

The sluice he had opened afterwards, and shut again, to put moving water and a wet coping into the night's story; the forged line he had written before dawn at his loft desk, in his pocket ink, copying the registrar's hand from a summer of watching her counter. He had known the forms exactly. He had not thought once of the moon.

CHAPTER XVI

The assizes would have Severin Quenholt at the spring sitting, and what the law would do with him the village did not yet know and Maren did not let herself guess. The Merrow Bell's underwriters sent a dry man in a city coat who spent two days with the tobacco-tin accounts and went away again; the salvage rights were forfeit; the net-loft was sealed with the magistrate's wax, and the gulls stood on its roof ridge as if appointed.

Lessa Pellow buried her brother on the headland side of the churchyard, where the stones lean east with the weather, and went back to her light the same evening, because the light does not choose, and does not stop.

Maren Ashquill went back to her ledger.

There was an entry to make that no column had been ruled for, and she made it in the remarks space at the foot of the night page for the fourteenth, beneath the forged line, which the magistrate had ordered must stay in the book — struck through in red, attested by three signatures, but legible, because a record that pretends it was never lied to is itself a lie. She wrote the plain facts: the line above was forged, by whom, proven how; the chronometer recovered and rehung; the survey of the Merrow Bell held at last, an empty hold opened to the light. She wrote it in iron-gall ink, and watched the brown-black bite into the paper, going darker as it dried, the way the truth settles.

CHAPTER XI

The basin gave up its second witness on the fifth day, when the constable had the sluice culvert and the silt grate dragged.

The silt grate was an iron lattice at the basin's deep corner, where the scour of years had piled a black ooze of weed and grit, and what came up from it, among the bottle glass and the lost shackles, were two things. The first was a boat-hook — not a quay boat-hook, but a heavy salvage pattern with a riveted iron head, and on the ash shaft, stamped deep and filled with old paint, the letters M.B. Tabb Orrison, who had helped stow the Merrow Bell's recovered gear a dozen times that summer, knew the stamp at sight: it was the mark the salvage crew struck into everything raised from the wreck. The hook was from the Merrow Bell's own salvage gear, out of the net-loft stores.

The second thing was small, and it was Maren who understood it. Caught in the grate's lattice, bright among the black ooze, lay a knurled brass button the size of a thumbnail: the winding-crown of a chronometer, snapped off at the stem. She turned it in her palm and felt the breakage rough under her thumb, and she thought of the empty walnut case on the office wall.

Doctor Fosk, shown the boat-hook, set its riveted head against his measurements of the wound and would commit himself no further than a dry man ever commits himself: the iron edge of such a head, he said, answered the wound at the temple in width, in depth, and in the clean line of it, as the rounded coping stones did not.

The ink was proven in Doctor Fosk's surgery at Saltern Cross, on a deal table cleared of its bottles, with Constable Marlock and Maren for witnesses and the tide ledger lying open at the night page under the doctor's good lamp.

Doctor Fosk was no chemist by trade, but a coroner's surgeon on a smuggling coast learns paper the way he learns knife wounds. He worked with a camel-hair brush, a saucer of weak acid, and the patience of a man poaching an egg. The lock basin at Glasswater Stave held its water the way the village held its opinions: behind heavy gates, and grudgingly. A Tale of Glasswater Stave

CHAPTER I

The lock basin at Glasswater Stave held its water the way the village held its opinions: behind heavy gates, and grudgingly. At slack water on a grey morning the basin was a rectangle of pewter, walled in dressed stone, crossed by the shadows of mooring posts, and smelling of weed and tar and the cold iron of the sluice machinery. It was Tabb Orrison who found the harbormaster floating in it, a little after dawn, while the gulls were still arguing over the fish-gutting boards on the quay.

Tabb was the lock-keeper's apprentice, seventeen years old and not yet used to the idea that the sea kept no appointments. He had come down to grease the pawls of the eastern gate, as he did every third morning, and he saw first the harbormaster's coat — a good drab coat with horn buttons, spread on the water like a chart of some unlucky coast — and then the white hair, and then the face. He did not shout at once. He told Constable Marlock afterwards that the silence of it had seemed to forbid shouting, that the basin at slack water was like a church with the sexton drowned in the font. Then the cold sense of things returned to him and he ran up the quay yelling for help with his grease-can still in one hand.

Corwin Pellow had been harbormaster of Glasswater Stave for twenty-one years. He had a square, patient face, a habit of writing everything down, and a reputation along the whole Hethering coast for being un-bribable, which in a salvage port is a reputation with enemies attached to it. Glasswater Stave is not on the railway, and the coast road reaches it as if by afterthought, dropping off the saltgrass downs in eleven bends that the carrier's van takes at a walk. Glasswater Stave is not on the railway, and the coast road reaches it as if by afterthought, dropping off the saltgrass downs in eleven bends that the carrier's van takes at a walk. The village is one street deep along the harbor and two streets deep behind it, built of the grey stone of the district, roofed in slate the weather has rubbed to the color of a herring's back. What it has always had, and the reason there is a village at all, is the inner harbor: a pool of still water behind lock gates, where a vessel can lie afloat at any state of the tide while the sea outside falls away down the mud at low water for half a mile.

The lock is the village's heart, and the village keeps its heart under administration. The gates and the sluice belong to the harbor trust; the lock-keeper works them; the harbormaster commands them; and the tide-registrar records them. Strangers find the arrangement quaint until they have wintered there. On the Hethering coast the difference between a harbor with honest books and a harbor without them is the difference between credit and none: the underwriters' agents, the salvage buyers, the fish merchants up the coast — all of them deal with Glasswater Stave on the strength of its paper. A master who declares his catch there is believed at the weighbridge in Saltern Cross. A salvage lot surveyed there sells unseen. The village does not put it this way, but its ledgers are its fishery as much as the sea is.

Salvage is the district's other trade, and the less talked of. A broker who lands his recoveries at Glasswater Stave pays for the privilege of being believed. Of the sea itself the village holds the views of people who live by a great unreliable neighbor. The tides at Glasswater Stave run twenty feet at the springs and barely nine at the neaps, and every trade in the port is timed to that fortnightly breathing. Doctor Imbrey Fosk came over from Saltern Cross in his rattling motor-trap and made his examination on the weighing platform with the crowd pushed back to the chandlery wall. He was a long, dry, exact man who had been coroner's surgeon for the district longer than anyone could remember, and he did not talk while he worked. When he had finished he washed his hands in a bucket of seawater, dried them on his handkerchief, and gave Constable Marlock his findings in a voice pitched for the constable alone, though half the quay contrived to hear it.

Drowning, said Doctor Fosk, was the cause of death; the harbormaster's lungs had taken water, and he had been alive when he went in. But the wound at the temple had been got before the water, not in it. The coping stones of the basin were rounded and weeded; a fall against them would bruise and graze. This wound was narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged — struck, in the doctor's opinion, by an iron edge swung with force. A man so struck might be stunned past saving himself, and the basin would do the rest.

"Then it's murder," said Constable Marlock. He was a heavy, careful man who had policed the village for nine years, mostly against poachers and Saturday fights, and he said the word the way a man picks up an unfamiliar tool.

"It is drowning, with a blow before it," said Doctor Fosk. "The arrangement of those two facts is your trade, Constable, not mine."

CHAPTER VII

The inquest on Corwin Pellow was held on the third day, in the long room of The Cold Lantern, because the village had no other room that would hold the crowd. The coroner came out from Saltern Cross; the jury were seven men and two women of the village, sworn on the inn's own Bible with the fish-scale still under their nails; and Widow Hetch shut the bar for the duration, which the older men counted the most serious mark of the occasion.

Tabb Orrison gave his evidence first, twisting his cap, and was treated gently. He told how he had come down at first light to grease the pawls of the eastern gate; how he had seen the coat on the water and then the white hair; how he had run up the quay shouting with the grease-can still in his hand. Asked by the coroner whether the basin had shown anything else amiss, he said the water had stood high on the gauge for the time of month, which he had thought strange even in his fright, the tides then being at the neaps, and the gates shut fast since the Saltwillow came through on the evening of the fourteenth.

Doctor Imbrey Fosk gave the medical evidence in the dry, complete manner of long practice, and the long room was silent under it. Death by drowning, the lungs taking water, the man alive when he entered the basin. A wound at the right temple, got before the water: narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged, made by an iron edge swung with force, and not to be had from any fall against rounded and weeded coping stones. CHAPTER IX

In the middle of that week the village contrived to frighten itself with a second mystery, which is worth setting down because of what it shows about the temper of a place where murder has come ashore.

The chandlery at Glasswater Stave is kept by the Brisk family, and has been since the trust was chartered; it sells everything a port wants, from stone bottles of the registrar's ink to tarred twine, and its store-room runs back into the rock of the hill itself. On the Wednesday morning young Mrs Brisk opened the store-room and found the brass spirit-lamp gone from its shelf — the big swinging lamp off the wrecked steamer Carnholm, which had hung there a dozen years waiting for a buyer who never came. The shelf was dusty; the dust was disturbed; the store-room window, which had not been opened in the memory of the trade, stood unlatched.

She had been a familiar of the port for years: a coasting ketch of ninety tons, broad in the bow, slow and sure, working general cargoes up and down the Hethering coast in all weathers. Her master had used Glasswater Stave through every season and knew the Saltgrass shoals, the village would have said, as well as any man who did not actually fish them. answer:
**What was stolen from the harbormaster's office:**

The object stolen was a **Lyle-Hannett chronometer**, specifically its travelling box and instrument. The passages state: "Under a hand's depth of coarse salt, wrapped in oiled canvas and a salvage flag, lay the travelling box of the Lyle-Hannett chronometer, and in the box the chronometer itself" [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. 

Evidence supporting this includes:
- A knurled brass button (the winding-crown) found snapped off at the stem among debris in the silt grate [Source: saltgrass-ledger]
- Doctor Fosk confirmed that an iron edge from a boat-hook answered the wound at the harbormaster's temple with width, depth, and clean line matching such a head [Source: saltgrass-ledger]
- The chronometer was recovered from Severin Quenholt's net-loft after he had hidden it under salt to avoid detection as stolen property "too known to sell" [Source: saltgrass-ledger]

**What made up the Merrow Bell's insured cargo:**

The passages do not specify what particular goods constituted the Merrow Bell's insurance. They only state that she carried **"general cargoes"** — described in one passage as working "general cargoes up and down the Hethering coast" [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. 

Regarding her specific contents at the time of loss, the text notes that when wrecked on October 14th (the year before), she was carrying an **insured cargo in her hold**, which had been paid out by underwriters to Severin Quenholt for salvage purposes [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. However, this cargo never arrived at any quay or lighter because it had already been stolen from the ship while still underwater.

The passages clarify that Quenholt's divers stripped the hold quietly in spring after the wreck, selling the goods twice over — first to insurers and then to buyers "in the dark" — leaving the actual physical merchandise unstated but confirmed as having existed and being insured [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

THE SALTGRASS LEDGER

A Tale of Glasswater Stave

CHAPTER I

The lock basin at Glasswater Stave held its water the way the village held its opinions: behind heavy gates, and grudgingly. At slack water on a grey morning the basin was a rectangle of pewter, walled in dressed stone, crossed by the shadows of mooring posts, and smelling of weed and tar and the cold iron of the sluice machinery. It was Tabb Orrison who found the harbormaster floating in it, a little after dawn, while the gulls were still arguing over the fish-gutting boards on the quay.

Tabb was the lock-keeper's apprentice, seventeen years old and not yet used to the idea that the sea kept no appointments. He had come down to grease the pawls of the eastern gate, as he did every third morning, and he saw first the harbormaster's coat — a good drab coat with horn buttons, spread on the water like a chart of some unlucky coast — and then the white hair, and then the face. He did not shout at once. He told Constable Marlock afterwards that the silence of it had seemed to forbid shouting, that the basin at slack water was like a church with the sexton drowned in the font. Then the cold sense of things returned to him and he ran up the quay yelling for help with his grease-can still in one hand.

Corwin Pellow had been harbormaster of Glasswater Stave for twenty-one years. He had a square, patient face, a habit of writing everything down, and a reputation along the whole Hethering coast for being un-bribable, which in a salvage port is a reputation with enemies attached to it. Glasswater Stave is not on the railway, and the coast road reaches it as if by afterthought, dropping off the saltgrass downs in eleven bends that the carrier's van takes at a walk. The village is one street deep along the harbor and two streets deep behind it, built of the grey stone of the district, roofed in slate the weather has rubbed to the color of a herring's back. What it has always had, and the reason there is a village at all, is the inner harbor: a pool of still water behind lock gates, where a vessel can lie afloat at any state of the tide while the sea outside falls away down the mud at low water for half a mile.

The lock is the village's heart, and the village keeps its heart under administration. The gates and the sluice belong to the harbor trust; the lock-keeper works them; the harbormaster commands them; and the tide-registrar records them. Strangers find the arrangement quaint until they have wintered there. On the Hethering coast the difference between a harbor with honest books and a harbor without them is the difference between credit and none: the underwriters' agents, the salvage buyers, the fish merchants up the coast — all of them deal with Glasswater Stave on the strength of its paper. A master who declares his catch there is believed at the weighbridge in Saltern Cross. A salvage lot surveyed there sells unseen. The village does not put it this way, but its ledgers are its fishery as much as the sea is.

In the middle of that week the village contrived to frighten itself with a second mystery, which is worth setting down because of what it shows about the temper of a place where murder has come ashore.

The shelf was dusty; the dust was disturbed; the store-room window, which had not been opened in the memory of the trade, stood unlatched.

Constable Marlock, meanwhile, had arrested no one, but he had come as near to it as made the village hold its breath: he had taken Tabb Orrison into the back room of the constabulary cottage and kept him there an afternoon.

The forged line recorded a sluice opening; the sluice was the lock-keeper's machinery; the lock-keeper was old and slept like the dead, and his apprentice held the keys and the grease-can and knew every pawl and winch of the gates. Tabb had access to the basin at all hours. Tabb had found the body — and the man who finds the body, said the constable's notebook, must always account for himself. CHAPTER XI

The basin gave up its second witness on the fifth day, when the constable had the sluice culvert and the silt grate dragged.

The silt grate was an iron lattice at the basin's deep corner, where the scour of years had piled a black ooze of weed and grit, and what came up from it, among the bottle glass and the lost shackles, were two things. The first was a boat-hook — not a quay boat-hook, but a heavy salvage pattern with a riveted iron head, and on the ash shaft, stamped deep and filled with old paint, the letters M.B. Tabb Orrison, who had helped stow the Merrow Bell's recovered gear a dozen times that summer, knew the stamp at sight: it was the mark the salvage crew struck into everything raised from the wreck. The hook was from the Merrow Bell's own salvage gear, out of the net-loft stores.

The second thing was small, and it was Maren who understood it. Caught in the grate's lattice, bright among the black ooze, lay a knurled brass button the size of a thumbnail: the winding-crown of a chronometer, snapped off at the stem. She turned it in her palm and felt the breakage rough under her thumb, and she thought of the empty walnut case on the office wall.

Doctor Fosk, shown the boat-hook, set its riveted head against his measurements of the wound and would commit himself no further than a dry man ever commits himself: the iron edge of such a head, he said, answered the wound at the temple in width, in depth, and in the clean line of it, as the rounded coping stones did not.

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. It was a marine chronometer of the old proud kind, brass-bound in a case of black walnut, made by the firm of Lyle & Hannett whose name was engraved across its face in letters like a ship's transom. Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

They took Severin Quenholt at The Cold Lantern that evening, where he sat at his usual table with his usual glass, agreeing pleasantly with his neighbors about the sad state of the times.

He denied nothing for long; that was the strangest part, the village said afterwards, and the part that made it believable. Confronted in the inn's back parlor with the chronometer, the tobacco-tin accounts, the boat-hook stamped M.B., and the doctor's saucer of violet-blooming ink, he sat quiet for a while with his hands folded, like a merchant checking a column twice, and then he balanced the books aloud.

He had gone to the harbor office late on the fourteenth to reason with Pellow, he said — only to reason, to offer the survey a percentage of its own. The harbormaster had listened with his patient square face and then said he would have the registrar's ledger in on Monday, the original, and the survey held in the open, and the books set side by side; paper was honest, said the harbormaster, even on this quay. Then he had turned to take the chronometer's travelling box down — the survey would need official time, he said, everything would be done by the book — and something in the calm of it, said Quenholt, in the man's untroubled certainty that figures must come right, had risen over him like water over a gauge. The boat-hook had been standing against his own barrow of salvage gear by the door. He did not remember deciding.

The sluice he had opened afterwards, and shut again, to put moving water and a wet coping into the night's story; the forged line he had written before dawn at his loft desk, in his pocket ink, copying the registrar's hand from a summer of watching her counter. THE SALTGRASS LEDGER

A Tale of Glasswater Stave

CHAPTER I

The lock basin at Glasswater Stave held its water the way the village held its opinions: behind heavy gates, and grudgingly. At slack water on a grey morning the basin was a rectangle of pewter, walled in dressed stone, crossed by the shadows of mooring posts, and smelling of weed and tar and the cold iron of the sluice machinery. It was Tabb Orrison who found the harbormaster floating in it, a little after dawn, while the gulls were still arguing over the fish-gutting boards on the quay.

Tabb was the lock-keeper's apprentice, seventeen years old and not yet used to the idea that the sea kept no appointments. He had come down to grease the pawls of the eastern gate, as he did every third morning, and he saw first the harbormaster's coat — a good drab coat with horn buttons, spread on the water like a chart of some unlucky coast — and then the white hair, and then the face. He did not shout at once. He told Constable Marlock afterwards that the silence of it had seemed to forbid shouting, that the basin at slack water was like a church with the sexton drowned in the font. Then the cold sense of things returned to him and he ran up the quay yelling for help with his grease-can still in one hand.

Corwin Pellow had been harbormaster of Glasswater Stave for twenty-one years. He had a square, patient face, a habit of writing everything down, and a reputation along the whole Hethering coast for being un-bribable, which in a salvage port is a reputation with enemies attached to it. The village brought him out of the basin with a pair of gaffs and laid him on the weighing platform by the fish scales, and by seven o'clock the whole of Glasswater Stave knew that the harbormaster was drowned, and by half past seven the whole village had privately decided it was no accident, though nobody would say so above a whisper until the doctor had had his look.

He trusted records the way other men trusted luck. It was the thing they had agreed about without ever needing to say so.

Glasswater Stave is not on the railway, and the coast road reaches it as if by afterthought, dropping off the saltgrass downs in eleven bends that the carrier's van takes at a walk. The village is one street deep along the harbor and two streets deep behind it, built of the grey stone of the district, roofed in slate the weather has rubbed to the color of a herring's back. What it has always had, and the reason there is a village at all, is the inner harbor: a pool of still water behind lock gates, where a vessel can lie afloat at any state of the tide while the sea outside falls away down the mud at low water for half a mile.

The lock is the village's heart, and the village keeps its heart under administration. The gates and the sluice belong to the harbor trust; the lock-keeper works them; the harbormaster commands them; and the tide-registrar records them. Strangers find the arrangement quaint until they have wintered there. On the Hethering coast the difference between a harbor with honest books and a harbor without them is the difference between credit and none: the underwriters' agents, the salvage buyers, the fish merchants up the coast — all of them deal with Glasswater Stave on the strength of its paper. A master who declares his catch there is believed at the weighbridge in Saltern Cross. A salvage lot surveyed there sells unseen. The village does not put it this way, but its ledgers are its fishery as much as the sea is.

CHAPTER IV

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. It was a marine chronometer of the old proud kind, brass-bound in a case of black walnut, made by the firm of Lyle & Hannett whose name was engraved across its face in letters like a ship's transom. It had come off a wrecked Indiaman sixty years before, had been bought at the salvage auction by the village trust, and had hung on the office wall ever since as the official timepiece of the port of Glasswater Stave. Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

Now the walnut case hung open and the chronometer was gone, and the dust on the shelf below showed the clean square where its travelling box had stood.

"Thieves, then," said Constable Marlock, writing in his notebook. "He surprised a thief at the office, and was struck, and put in the basin."

"Then the thief," said Maren, "knew enough to take the travelling box, which was kept in the cupboard, and to take the winding key, which was kept in the desk; and knew nothing about the cash drawer, which was not even locked. That is a thief with strange priorities, Constable."

The constable looked at the cash drawer, which held four pounds and some silver, untouched, and wrote in his notebook again, more slowly.

Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

They took Severin Quenholt at The Cold Lantern that evening, where he sat at his usual table with his usual glass, agreeing pleasantly with his neighbors about the sad state of the times.

The Lyle-Hannett chronometer was the only valuable thing in the harbormaster's office, and the only beautiful one. Every opening of the lock was timed by it. Every entry in Maren's tide ledger carried a time taken from it. Corwin Pellow wound it himself every Monday noon, with a ceremony he pretended was not a ceremony.

Now the walnut case hung open and the chronometer was gone, and the dust on the shelf below showed the clean square where its travelling box had stood.

"Thieves, then," said Constable Marlock, writing in his notebook. "He surprised a thief at the office, and was struck, and put in the basin."

question: Give a complete account of the Merrow Bell insurance fraud, in sections: what specific goods made up her insured cargo, how and when that cargo was stripped from the wreck and disposed of, in what year the ship was lost, and how the fraud was finally proved.

Based on the provided text from *saltgrass-ledger*, here is an account of the Merrow Bell insurance fraud.

### The Year and Circumstances of Loss
The ship *Merrow Bell* was lost in **October** (the specific year is not stated, only that it occurred "the year before" the autumn investigation). She went down during a severe gale with rain like shot, after striking the Saltgrass shoals two miles east of Wrack Point. Her crew escaped in their dinghy, but the ninety-ton ketch sank quickly into eight fathoms of water [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

### Insured Cargo
The text identifies the insured cargo as **"general cargoes"** loaded at Saltern Cross for trade up and down the Hethering coast [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. The narrative does not provide an itemized manifest or list specific goods (such as grain, timber, or textiles) that made up this general cargo; it refers to them collectively as "the meat" of her hold, distinct from the ship's own gear and furniture ("bones") which were later raised [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

### Stripping and Disposal of the Cargo
The fraud was orchestrated by **Severin Quenholt**, a salvage broker who had purchased the wreck from the underwriters. 
*   **Stripping:** Before the official survey could take place, Quenholt’s divers quietly stripped the insured cargo from the hold in the spring. The text notes they worked "quietly," suggesting covert removal rather than open looting [Source: saltgrass-ledger].
*   **Disposal:** Once removed, the goods were transported up the coast in small lots through other ports (avoiding Glasswater Stave). They were sold twice over: once to insurers via the fraudulent loss claim, and again to private buyers on the dark market ("sold... to the buyers in the dark") [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

### How the Fraud Was Proved
The fraud was exposed by **Maren Ashquill** (the registrar) and **Constable Marlock**, following the murder of the harbormaster, Corwin Pellow. The proof relied on three converging pieces of evidence:
1.  **The Tide Ledger:** Maren discovered a forged entry added to her tide ledger after Pellow’s death. It claimed the basin sluice had been opened at night to scour weed—a claim that contradicted the physical reality of the tides and proved someone had tampered with records to hide activity in the port [Source: saltgrass-ledger].
2.  **The Chronometer:** A Lyle-Hannett chronometer was stolen from Pellow's office during his murder. Quenholt kept it hidden under coarse salt in a salvage barrel, believing its absence would be forgotten or attributed to simple theft rather than fraud. However, he wound it while waiting for the scandal to die down; Maren found the broken winding-crown stem inside this very chronometer when she inspected the salt barrel at the net-loft [Source: saltgrass-ledger].
3.  **The Broker’s Accounts:** Hidden alongside the chronometer in oiled canvas and a tobacco tin were "the broker's true accounts of the Merrow Bell" written by Quenholt himself. These figures proved that the insured cargo had never been on board during the loss (or was stripped before) and detailed how the goods had been sold twice over [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

When Pellow threatened to conduct an official survey, which would have revealed an empty hold ([unverified excerpt: an empty hold opened under the eyes of the law]), he was murdered. The discovery of his own ledger entry—forged by Quenholt—and the recovered false accounts allowed Maren to prove that the *Merrow Bell*’s hold was effectively empty when raised, exposing the insurance scam [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

answer:
The Cold Lantern was the village inn, its long room serving as the inquest chamber and later the scene of Quenholt’s arrest. The landlady is **Widow Hetch** — she “shut the bar for the duration” when the inquest began, marking it with older men considered “the most serious mark of the occasion.”

## In the Long Room: The Inquest (Chapter VII)
The coroner came from Saltern Cross; the jury were seven men and two women sworn on the inn’s own Bible with fish-scale still under their nails. Evidence included:
- Tabb Orrison testified he saw Corwin Pellow’s coat on water at first light, then white hair; he noted the basin showed high tide despite neap tides (“which he had thought strange even in his fright”).
- Doctor Imbrey Fosk gave medical evidence: death by drowning, lungs taking water, man alive when entering the basin. A wound at the right temple was “narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged, made by an iron edge swung with force,” not from falling against rounded coping stones. The doctor said a struck man might be insensible past saving himself in two feet of water, let alone the basin’s twelve. He added that men do not commonly strike themselves above the ear with an iron edge and then arrange to drown.
- Constable Marlock testified gates were shut and pawled, sluice shut; harbormaster’s office found locked next morning with cash drawer untouched; port’s chronometer missing — travelling box and winding key gone.
- Registrar Maren Ashquill confirmed ledger heights for the fourteenth but was not asked about pages further (constable requested documents not canvassed in open court).

The jury returned “wilful murder” after twenty minutes out. The coroner adjourned *sine die*, released the body, and left before dark. The bar reopened within the hour; the long room echoed with the word “murder.”

## In the Back Parlor: Quenholt’s Arrest and Confession (Chapter XV)
Severin Quenholt was taken to The Cold Lantern that evening where he sat at his usual table with his usual glass, agreeing pleasantly with neighbors about the sad state of times. Confronted in the back parlor with evidence — chronometer, tobacco-tin accounts, boat-hook stamped M.B., doctor’s saucer of violet-blooming ink — he denied nothing for a while (“the strangest part”). He then balanced books aloud:
- Claimed he went late on the fourteenth to reason with Pellow, offering survey percentage; harbormaster asked for registrar’s ledger original and open survey side by side (“paper is honest”) before taking down chronometer travelling box.
- Said something “rose over him like water over a gauge” when Pellow took the chronometer; boat-hook had been standing against his barrow of salvage gear by door; he did not remember deciding.
- Admitted opening sluice afterwards to put moving water into story; forged line written at loft desk in pocket ink copying registrar’s hand from summer watching her counter. He knew forms exactly but never thought of moon or tide — noting twenty years brokering wrecks without learning water, while Pellow would have checked almanac first.

In the middle of that week the village contrived to frighten itself with a second mystery, which is worth setting down because of what it shows about the temper of a place where murder has come ashore.

The night the Merrow Bell was lost had entered the parish memory before that autumn gave the loss its second meaning, and the account of it belongs here, as the village would tell it.

She had been a familiar of the port for years: a coasting ketch of ninety tons, broad in the bow, slow and sure, working general cargoes up and down the Hethering coast in all weathers. Constable Marlock, the heavy and careful constable of Glasswater Stave who had policed the village for nine years [Source: saltgrass-ledger], conducted his investigation into the death of harbormaster Corwin Pellow through a methodical sequence of evidence gathering, interrogation, and forensic verification.

**1. Initial Examination and Scene Assessment (Day 1)**
Marlock’s conduct began at the weighing platform where Doctor Imbrey Fosk examined Pellow’s body. The doctor determined that while drowning was the cause of death, a clean-edged wound to the temple—inflicted by an iron edge swung with force before entering the water—indicated murder [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Marlock accepted this finding ("Then it's murder") and immediately began securing the scene [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. He verified the state of the lock gates, which had been shut since the evening of the fourteenth when the ketch *Saltwillow* passed through [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

**2. Witness Interviews and Discovery of Missing Property (Day 1)**
Marlock took evidence from Widow Hetch at The Cold Lantern, who confirmed Pellow was seen alive at nine o'clock on the night of his death, appearing "heavy in his mind" for a fortnight due to issues with the salvage survey of the wrecked *Merrow Bell* [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Marlock then accompanied Maren Ashquill, the tide-registrar, into the harbormaster’s office. There, he discovered that the Lyle-Hannett chronometer—the port's official timepiece—was missing along with its travelling box and winding key, while the cash drawer (containing four pounds) remained untouched [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. This discrepancy led him to initially suspect a thief who had surprised Pellow [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

**3. Interrogation of Tabb Orrison (Day 2)**
Marlock arrested Tabb Orrison, the lock-keeper’s apprentice, and detained him in the back room of the constabulary cottage for an afternoon [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Marlock reasoned that Orrison had access to the basin at all hours, knew every pawl and winch of the gates, and was found with the body; furthermore, Orrison had been seen on the quay past eleven o'clock despite claiming to be abed [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. During questioning, Orrison contradicted himself regarding his whereabouts but admitted anyone could copy the registrar's hand because the ledger lay open half the day [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. However, Maren Ashquill intervened, pointing out that a forged entry in the ledger recorded a sluice opening during a neap tide—a hydrological impossibility for scouring—proving the forger lacked knowledge of the sea [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Marlock accepted this deduction, shifting suspicion away from Orrison toward someone who knew office forms but not tides [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

**4. Forensic Analysis of Evidence (Day 5-8)**
On the fifth day, Marlock ordered the dragging of the basin’s silt grate and sluice culvert [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. This yielded two critical items: a salvage boat-hook stamped "M.B." (from the *Merrow Bell*) and a knurled brass chronometer winding-crown snapped off at the stem [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Doctor Fosk confirmed the boat-hook’s iron edge matched Pellow’s temple wound in width, depth, and clean line [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

Marlock then facilitated the ink analysis conducted by Doctor Fosk on Maren Ashquill’s ledger. The doctor proved that the forged entry was written with logwood ink—a dye-black that sits on paper—rather than the office's standard iron-gall ink which bites into fiber [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. This established the forgery was recent (barely settled) and committed by someone using a travelling man's pocket bottle of ink [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Marlock recorded these findings meticulously in his notebook [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

**5. Search and Arrest (Day 8)**
On the eighth day, Constable Marlock obtained a magistrate’s warrant from Saltern Cross to search Severin Quenholt’s net-loft at the south end of the quay [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. While searching salvage barrels, Maren Ashquill discovered the chronometer hidden inside a salt barrel stenciled with "Merrow Bell" [Source: saltgrass-ledger]. Confronted with the recovered chronometer, tobacco-tin accounts, the stamped boat-hook, and the forensic evidence of the logwood ink forgery in his loft, Severin Quenholt was arrested that evening at The Cold Lantern where he had been sitting pleasantly with neighbors [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

**Conclusion**
Quenholt confessed to striking Pellow with the boat-hook after being overwhelmed by the harbormaster's untroubled certainty about exposing Quenholt’s salvage fraud. He opened the sluice to stage a drowning scene and forged the ledger entry using pocket ink before dawn [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

Severin Quenholt faced trial at the spring assizes; however, the provided text does not specify the exact sentence (e.g., length of imprisonment or death) he received at that sitting, only noting that "what the law would do with him the village did not yet know" [Source: saltgrass-ledger].

In the spring the underwriters had sold their interest in the wreck, as underwriters do, to whoever would gamble on raising what the sea had kept. The gambler was Severin Quenholt.

Quenholt was the salvage broker of Glasswater Stave. He was a wide, soft-stepping man of fifty with a fair beard going grey and a manner of agreeing with everyone so pleasantly that it took a careful listener to notice he had promised nothing. He held the salvage rights of half the bad ground on the Hethering coast; he bought wrecks the way other men bought standing timber, and his lugger and his hired divers worked them through the fair months. He kept the net-loft at the south end of the quay as his store, and what came up from the sea — chain, anchors, copper, cargo — went into the net-loft and out again to buyers up the coast, and a fixed percentage went, as the law required, through the harbormaster's survey.

That was the rub, and the village knew it without being told. For a salvage cargo landed at Glasswater Stave, Corwin Pellow's signature was worth money: his survey fixed what had been recovered and what it weighed, and the harbormaster's book and the broker's book had to agree. For twenty-one years they always had. CHAPTER VI

The night page for the fourteenth had five entries, and Maren Ashquill had written four of them.

She knew her own hand the way she knew her own walk, and she knew the office ink. The first four entries — the Saltwillow through the lock on the flood, the gates wound to behind her, the height at the gauge, the watch handed to the night man — stood in iron-gall brown, bitten well into the paper, already going dark with age as iron-gall does in its first weeks. The fifth entry was not hers.

It was a good forgery; she gave it that much, professionally, the way a wronged carpenter might admire the joinery of the man who robbed him. The hand was a studied copy of her own upright round-hand. The ruling was respected, the abbreviations were correct, even the registrar's tick in the margin was copied. It recorded, in eleven words, that the lock sluice had been opened at half past eleven on the night of the fourteenth to scour weed from the basin, on the harbormaster's verbal order, and shut again at midnight.

CHAPTER III

Doctor Imbrey Fosk came over from Saltern Cross in his rattling motor-trap and made his examination on the weighing platform with the crowd pushed back to the chandlery wall. He was a long, dry, exact man who had been coroner's surgeon for the district longer than anyone could remember, and he did not talk while he worked. When he had finished he washed his hands in a bucket of seawater, dried them on his handkerchief, and gave Constable Marlock his findings in a voice pitched for the constable alone, though half the quay contrived to hear it.

Drowning, said Doctor Fosk, was the cause of death; the harbormaster's lungs had taken water, and he had been alive when he went in. But the wound at the temple had been got before the water, not in it. The coping stones of the basin were rounded and weeded; a fall against them would bruise and graze. This wound was narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged — struck, in the doctor's opinion, by an iron edge swung with force. A man so struck might be stunned past saving himself, and the basin would do the rest.

"Then it's murder," said Constable Marlock. He was a heavy, careful man who had policed the village for nine years, mostly against poachers and Saturday fights, and he said the word the way a man picks up an unfamiliar tool.

Maren Ashquill heard the bell going on the quay and knew before anyone told her. She was the tide-registrar of Glasswater Stave — keeper of the tide ledger, recorder of every opening and shutting of the lock, every vessel through the gates, every height of water against the painted gauge on the basin wall. Her office was a square stone room at the head of the quay, between the harbormaster's office and the chandlery, and from its window she had watched Corwin Pellow cross the cobbles every working morning for eleven years, always at the same hour, always pausing at the gauge to verify her morning figure against his own eye. He trusted records the way other men trusted luck. It was the thing they had agreed about without ever needing to say so.

She came down to the weighing platform with her shawl pinned crooked and stood at the edge of the crowd while two fishermen kept the gulls off. The harbormaster's eyes were shut. There was a wound at his right temple, washed bloodless by the basin, the lips of it grey.

"He fell," said someone in the crowd, without conviction. "Slipped on the coping in the dark and fell."

Maren looked at the wound, and at the basin, and at the great closed gates of the lock, and said nothing at all. But she went back up to her office, and before the doctor had even been sent for she had taken down the tide ledger and turned to the night pages, because it was her habit, in any confusion, to begin with what was written down.

In the middle of that week the village contrived to frighten itself with a second mystery, which is worth setting down because of what it shows about the temper of a place where murder has come ashore.

The chandlery at Glasswater Stave is kept by the Brisk family, and has been since the trust was chartered; it sells everything a port wants, from stone bottles of the registrar's ink to tarred twine, and its store-room runs back into the rock of the hill itself. On the Wednesday morning young Mrs Brisk opened the store-room and found the brass spirit-lamp gone from its shelf — the big swinging lamp off the wrecked steamer Carnholm, which had hung there a dozen years waiting for a buyer who never came. CHAPTER VII

The inquest on Corwin Pellow was held on the third day, in the long room of The Cold Lantern, because the village had no other room that would hold the crowd. The coroner came out from Saltern Cross; the jury were seven men and two women of the village, sworn on the inn's own Bible with the fish-scale still under their nails; and Widow Hetch shut the bar for the duration, which the older men counted the most serious mark of the occasion.

Tabb Orrison gave his evidence first, twisting his cap, and was treated gently. He told how he had come down at first light to grease the pawls of the eastern gate; how he had seen the coat on the water and then the white hair; how he had run up the quay shouting with the grease-can still in his hand. Asked by the coroner whether the basin had shown anything else amiss, he said the water had stood high on the gauge for the time of month, which he had thought strange even in his fright, the tides then being at the neaps, and the gates shut fast since the Saltwillow came through on the evening of the fourteenth.

Doctor Imbrey Fosk gave the medical evidence in the dry, complete manner of long practice, and the long room was silent under it. Death by drowning, the lungs taking water, the man alive when he entered the basin. A wound at the right temple, got before the water: narrow, deep at one end, clean-edged, made by an iron edge swung with force, and not to be had from any fall against rounded and weeded coping stones. A man so struck, said the doctor, might be insensible past saving himself in two feet of water, let alone the basin's twelve.

Wrack Point light stood three miles east of the village on a shoulder of black rock, and Lessa Pellow kept it. She had been keeper there for six years — the Trinity men had made difficulties about a woman at first, and had then discovered, as Glasswater Stave could have told them, that difficulties made with a Pellow were difficulties wasted. She was the harbormaster's sister, younger by a dozen years, with the same square patient face, and she had the news of his death from the relief boat before noon of the first day.

Maren walked out to Wrack Point on the second evening, because the constable's inquiry moved at the speed of the constable and there were questions only a Pellow could answer.
